prompt: Right after my buy order fills, the shares appear in my demat account, so I can sell them today. Is that right?

options.text: Yes. An executed order is a holding.
No. The trade is cleared and settled first, and the holding appears after settlement [VERIFY: settlement timing].
Yes, but only for intraday trades.

explanations.a: Execution is not settlement. The trade is matched, then cleared, then settled, and the shares are credited after that.
explanations.c: Intraday positions are not delivery holdings. Delivery holdings appear after settlement, for any trade type (intraday positions are covered in T4.7).

options.text: Settlement on the next calendar day
Settlement one working day after the trade date [VERIFY: current rule and effective date]
Settlement two working days after the trade date
Settlement on the trade date itself

explanations.a: T+1 counts working days, not calendar days. Weekends and holidays are skipped.
explanations.c: Two working days would be a different cycle. The rule in this chapter is one working day after the trade date [VERIFY].
explanations.d: Settlement on the trade date would be T+0. T+1 is one working day later.

prompt: In one settlement cycle a broker has three buy trades of Rs 5,000 each and one sell trade of Rs 2,000. What is the net payable, in rupees, after netting?
solution: Gross buys = 3 x 5,000 = 15,000. Sell proceeds = 2,000. Net payable = 15,000 - 2,000 = Rs 13,000. Check: 13,000 + 2,000 = 15,000, which matches the gross buys. This is a concept illustration; the actual netting rules are [VERIFY: clearing corporation rules]. Common wrong answers: 17,000 (adds the sell instead of subtracting it) and 15,000 (ignores the sell).

prompt: Statement: 'My demat account holds my cash.' Which part of this statement is the mistake?

options.text: 'My demat account' (it does hold shares, so this part is correct)
'holds shares in electronic form' (this part is correct)

explanations.a: The demat account holds shares in electronic form. Naming it is correct; the error is what it is said to hold.
explanations.c: This describes the demat account correctly. The error is the claim about cash.

prompt: You bought 20 shares today in delivery and want to sell them tomorrow for delivery. Which constraint applies first?

options.text: The shares must be credited to your demat account before a delivery sale [VERIFY: rule on selling shares not yet credited].
No constraint. You can sell any time.
The shares must be sold before the market closes today.
Only the broker can decide when the sale is allowed.

explanations.b: A delivery sale depends on the shares being in your account, and the same-day assumption is a common mistake. Verify the rule first.
explanations.c: Closing time is not the constraint. The constraint is whether the shares are credited for delivery.
explanations.d: The broker passes on your order. The rule about crediting shares is set by the market rules, not by the broker's choice.

options.text: Settles every trade separately at its full value.
Reduces the many trades in one settlement cycle to a single net obligation for each security and each cash amount.
Removes the need for a bank account.

explanations.a: Settling every trade separately is the opposite of netting. Netting offsets trades before money or shares move, so the net figure is what changes hands [VERIFY: actual netting rules].
explanations.c: The linked bank account still moves the money. Netting reduces the number of obligations; it does not remove the need for funds.
